tagline: An old copper railway becomes a road across a bird-rich delta.
intro: The Copper River Highway leaves Cordova past Eyak Lake and the airport, then turns to gravel across sloughs through Eyak Corporation land and Chugach National Forest. Alaska’s scenic-byways program highlights the old railroad route and a delta supporting more than 500,000 migratory birds. The failed bridge at Mile 36 stops the drive short of the Million Dollar Bridge. Cordova itself has no road connection to the rest of Alaska’s communities apart from Eyak; visitors arrive by plane or ferry before beginning this local highway journey.

From 1911 to 1938, the Copper River and Northwestern Railway brought copper ore to Cordova’s harbor. Highway construction began in 1945 with the aim of connecting Cordova to the state road system at Chitina. The 1964 earthquake halted construction and collapsed the Million Dollar Bridge’s north span. Permanent bridge repairs were completed in 2005, but the later failure at Bridge 339 cut road access again.

Begin at Cordova’s ferry terminal and travel through town before passing Eyak Lake and Merle K. Smith Airport. The road heads east, then northeast across the delta toward the impassable bridge. The Million Dollar Bridge remains farther along the former route, between Childs and Miles glaciers, with no road access.

moments.title: Cordova
moments.text: Cordova’s harbor became the outlet for copper from Kennecott. Michael James Heney bought land for the railway terminus after judging neighboring Katalla a poor harbor, and his crew organized the town in March 1906. The first town lots sold at auction in 1908 form the heart of present-day Cordova. Commercial fishing is now the main industry, with the fleet working Prince William Sound and the Copper River Delta. The town remains outside Alaska’s connected road network, reached by boat or aircraft. The Cordova Historical Museum includes exhibits on both the railway and the local fishing industry.

moments.title: Copper River Delta
moments.text: The Copper River Delta is both salmon country and a migration stopover. Its 584 square miles provide a home or stopping place for more than 500,000 migratory birds and belong to the Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve network. Spring migrants include western sandpipers, least sandpipers and dunlin. They stop to rest and feed before continuing north. The highway crosses several sloughs on its way east and northeast, following the lower part of the abandoned copper railway. Cordova’s annual Copper River Delta Shorebird Festival takes place in early May, with activities, workshops and bird-watching tours throughout the week.

moments.title: Million Dollar Bridge
moments.text: Ice was part of the engineering problem at the Million Dollar Bridge. Started in 1909 and in full service by July 1910, the crossing had to withstand icebergs up to 20 feet high moving in a seven-mile-per-hour current. Two of its piers required detached icebreakers. Its nickname came from the original construction cost of $1.4 million. Rail service ended in 1938, and conversion for highway use was completed in 1958. The 1964 earthquake displaced one span; permanent repairs followed in 2005. The repaired landmark lies beyond the later washout that cut off road access.

practical: Million Dollar Bridge: The failed bridge at Mile 36 is impassable. There is no road access to the Million Dollar Bridge. (checked 2026-10-11)
